To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

spatial representations of television sets were not influenced by the number of camera views used in filming, and that experience with a television program is a necessary, but not sufficient condition for spatial representations of the set.

1) experience watching the constrained-views shows is much more strongly associated than experience with the multiple views shows, 2) long term spatial memory can result from short term spatial coding of individual scene, 3) experience with a novel view of the constrained set does not facilitate correct responding, and 4) experience with multiple view shows does not facilitate correct responses.
“Long-term spatial memory is a function of short-term spatial coding, but only when spatial information is consistent across views.”
In summary, our research is concerned with
how people learn and use representations of the spatial environment.
the question: how does the brain represent the spatial layout of an environment?
the spatial representations of sets in long-running television programs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
spatial representations are not a product of the spatial structure of the environment, but rather are determined by the structure of the information presented in a series of views.
the spatial representations of the multiple-view sets are not as accurate and detailed as the spatial representations of constrained-view sets.

the results of this experiment are consistent with the hypothesis that long-term spatial memory can result from short term spatial coding of individual scene, but only when the views are generally consistent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
spatial representations of multiple-view sets do not appear to be learned from the same processes as spatial representations of constrained-view sets.
the spatial memories of experienced viewers are no better than those of novices, even when they are asked to judge relative directions on a set that they are highly familiar with.
long-term memory of spatial information is a function of the consistency of the information over time.
The main takeaway from our work is that
spatial memories are not formed by the accumulation of individual spatial experiences.
spatial memories are not always accurate and that they can be easily distorted by the way in which a space is depicted.
spatial memory is not a simple function of experience, but rather is a complex function of the nature of the experience.
